title: A finite integral model isolates a normalization prime
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian integral domain [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], where an integral domain is a nonzero commutative ring without zero divisors. Let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ be its field of fractions and $N\subseteq K$ its integral closure [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. For every prime ideal $Q\subset N$, there is an intermediate subring $R\subseteq C\subseteq N$, generated by finitely many elements as an $R$-algebra, such that, with $p=Q\cap C$, $Q$ is the unique prime of $N$ contracting to $p$. The local domain $C_p$ is Noetherian, $\dim C_p=\dim N_Q=\operatorname{ht}Q$, and $N_Q$ is the integral closure of $C_p$ in $K$. Localizations are taken at the complements of the named primes [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]; dimension and height are the suprema of lengths of strict prime chains [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring].

source.place: Swanson–Huneke, Integral Closure of Ideals, Rings, and Modules. Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), including the two conclusions following In particular. No finiteness of the full normalization is asserted. Author-hosted PDF read online at https://www.math.purdue.edu/~iswanso/book/SwansonHuneke.pdf; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Put $q=Q\cap R$. By [lem-trf-normalization-finite-prime-fibres], list the finitely many primes of $N$ over $q$ as $Q=Q_1,\ldots,Q_r$, without repetitions; $r\ge1$ because $Q$ is given. Every element of $N$ is integral over $R$ by [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-integral-incomparability] says that the distinct $Q_i$ are pairwise incomparable. In particular $Q\not\subseteq Q_i$ for $i\ge2$.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: If $r>1$, apply [lem-weil-pbc-prime-avoidance] in the ring $N$ with ideal $J=Q$ and the finite family $Q_2,\ldots,Q_r$. The noncontainments are those of Step 1 and every ideal in the family is prime. Obtain $x\in Q$ outside every $Q_i$ for $i\ge2$. If $r=1$, choose $x=0\in Q$; the avoidance requirement is empty.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: Set $C=R[x]\subseteq N$ and $p=Q\cap C$. This is a subring generated by one element over $R$ and is a domain as a subring of $K$. The contraction $p$ is prime: if a product of two elements of $C$ is in $p$, primality in $N$ puts one factor in $Q\cap C$. Suppose $Q'\subset N$ is prime and $Q'\cap C=p$. Contracting further gives $Q'\cap R=q$, so $Q'=Q_i$ for some $i$ by Step 1. Since $x\in p$, one has $x\in Q_i$; Step 2 excludes $i\ge2$. Thus $Q'=Q$, proving the required uniqueness.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: The evaluation map $R[T]\twoheadrightarrow C$, $T\mapsto x$, presents $C$ as a quotient of a one-variable polynomial ring. Hence [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian] makes $C$ Noetherian. Put $A=C_p$ and $S=C\setminus p$ as in [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. It is a local domain, and its fraction field is $K$: $R\subseteq A\subseteq K$ gives both fraction-field inclusions.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: The ring $A=C_p$ is Noetherian directly from the definition [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. For an ideal $J\subseteq C_p$, let $I=\{c\in C:c/1\in J\}$. For $c/s\in J$, multiplication by the unit $s/1$ gives $c\in I$; conversely each $c\in I$ has every $c/s\in J$. Thus $J=IC_p$. Finite generators of $I$ over $C$ therefore generate $J$ over $C_p$.

source.place: Tag 00FN, lemma-Noetherian-permanence, localization part; contracted-ideal argument written out.

proof.text: Let $D\subseteq K$ be the integral closure of $C$ in $K$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Each element of $N$ satisfies a monic equation over $R\subseteq C$, so $N\subseteq D$. The maps $R\to C$ and $C\to D$ are integral: for $C$ this follows from $C\subseteq N$, and for $D$ it is its definition. By [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive], $D$ is integral over $R$. Hence $D\subseteq N$, proving $D=N$.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-commutes-localization] to $C\subseteq K$ and $S=C\setminus p$. All elements of $S$ are nonzero, and they are units in $K$, so $S^{-1}K=K$ by the maps $a/s\mapsto a s^{-1}$ and $a\mapsto a/1$. With $D=N$ from Step 6, the cited theorem identifies $B=S^{-1}N\subseteq K$ with the integral closure of $A=C_p$ in $K$. In particular $A\subseteq B$ is injective and integral; integrality is part of the definition of integral closure [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure].

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-integral-maximal-contracts-maximal], every maximal ideal $M$ of $B$ contracts to the unique maximal ideal $pA$ of $A$. Apply the prime correspondence (1) in [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] to $N\to B=S^{-1}N$. Its hypotheses follow from the fraction description. It gives a prime $Q'=M\cap N$ disjoint from $S$ with $M=Q'B$. For $c\in C$, one has $c/1\in pA$ if and only if $c\in p$ by [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Consequently $Q'\cap C=p$. Step 3 forces $Q'=Q$. Thus every maximal ideal of $B$ equals $QB$. Such an ideal exists since $B$ is a nonzero ring (it embeds in $K$). Hence $B$ is local with unique maximal ideal $QB$.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: Inside $K$ one has $B=N_Q$. The inclusion $B\subseteq N_Q$ holds because $S\subseteq N\setminus Q$. Conversely, if $t\in N\setminus Q$, prime correspondence gives $t/1\notin QB$. It is a unit in the local ring $B$: otherwise its principal ideal would be proper, contained in a maximal ideal, contradicting uniqueness of $QB$. Thus each fraction $n/t\in N_Q$ already belongs to $B$. With Step 7 this proves that $N_Q$ is the integral closure of $C_p$ in $K$.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-dimension-equal] to the injective integral inclusion $A\subseteq B$ from Step 7. It gives $\dim C_p=\dim B=\dim N_Q$ using Step 9. The prime correspondence (1) in [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] for $N\to N_Q$ identifies primes of $N_Q$ with primes of $N$ contained in $Q$. Extension and contraction preserve inclusions, hence strict chains; any such finite chain can be ended at $Q$. Taking suprema of lengths, as in [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], gives $\dim N_Q=\operatorname{ht}Q$. These are all required equalities. If $Q=(0)$ the localization is $K$, of dimension zero; the single-prime case of Step 2 also covers a field base.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke Lemma 4.8.4, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 99), finite-fibre separation and localized integral-extension argument; local PDF WANTED, author PDF read online.
